purpose: Academic prose revision preserving frozen evidence and explicit limits; no AI-detector claim.

paragraphs.match: Routing feedback consumes radio capacity and may confuse missing evidence with forwarding failure. We evaluate receipt assisted feedback and a separate authenticated transport for frozen sensor-routing policies. The first experiment fixes the feedback ledger before 750 IEEE 802.15.4 simulation runs on 30 new fixtures, with active proof, naive passive, frozen prior and capacity matched policy controls. Under blackholes, delivery increases from 71.28% to 75.94% relative to active proofs, a paired gain of 4.67 percentage points (95% interval 2.36–6.97; Holm adjusted p=0.0161). Energy per delivered byte improves while total modeled radio energy increases slightly. A second protocol evaluates attention, multilayer perceptron and greedy routing in 180 runs using byte-serialized neighbor state, hop authentication, replay protection and signed sink receipts. Attention delivery is 81.61% in benign conditions and 61.11% with selective dropping; paired comparisons establish no superiority over the controls. Four virtual serial devices also exercise the host radio adapter and reveal a receive-time freshness bug, which is corrected. The corrected integration delivers all ten offered packets in that functional fixture. A separate four-board Cortex-M3 emulator executes compiled radio-interface firmware; all three host-policy controls deliver ten of ten packets. These results provide traceable feedback and implementation evidence while exposing transfer and attribution limits. Virtual serial interfaces and modeled radio energy do not establish physical board operation, measured energy consumption or absolute deadline compliance.
replacement: Routing feedback uses airtime, yet an absent observation may say little about whether a relay forwarded a packet. We examine receipt-assisted passive feedback and the transfer of frozen routing policies to an authenticated transport. A prespecified study comprises 750 IEEE 802.15.4 simulation runs on 30 new fixtures, with active-proof, naive-passive, frozen-prior and capacity-matched policy controls. Under blackholes, delivery rises from 71.28% with active proofs to 75.94% with censored passive feedback: a paired improvement of 4.67 percentage points (95% interval 2.36–6.97; Holm-adjusted p=0.0161). Energy per delivered byte falls, although total modeled radio energy increases slightly. A separate 180-run study evaluates attention, multilayer perceptron and greedy routing with serialized neighbor state, hop authentication, replay protection and signed sink receipts. Attention delivers 81.61% of packets in benign conditions and 61.11% under selective dropping; the paired comparisons do not establish an advantage over either control. Serial-interface tests reveal a receive-time freshness error, corrected before repeat testing. Compiled radio-interface firmware then runs on four emulated Cortex-M3 boards, with all three host-policy controls delivering ten of ten packets. The evidence supports the tested feedback replacement and verifies specific implementation paths. Physical-board operation, measured energy consumption and absolute deadline compliance remain unvalidated.

paragraphs.match: Multihop sensor routing relies on link estimates, path progress and control messages, as illustrated by RPL, expected transmission count and the Collection Tree Protocol [1, 2, 3]. Adding security evidence creates another dependency: an extra acknowledgment may increase confidence in one hop while occupying airtime needed by another packet. A mechanism should therefore be judged jointly by what it observes and what it sends.
replacement: Multihop sensor networks depend on link estimates, progress toward the sink and control traffic. RPL, expected transmission count and the Collection Tree Protocol use these ingredients in different ways [1, 2, 3]. Adding forwarding evidence changes the balance: an acknowledgment can improve confidence in a relay while consuming airtime that would otherwise carry data. Assessing a feedback mechanism therefore requires measuring both the information it provides and the traffic it creates.

paragraphs.match: Passive watchdog monitoring and explicit acknowledgment schemes have addressed forwarding misbehavior for decades [4, 5]. Overhearing establishes that a relay attempted transmission; it does not establish reception by the intended next hop. Conversely, silence can result from an unsuccessful first link, contention or missed reception. Treating every silence as a malicious action can change routing even in an attack free network. The present study examines that observation ambiguity without introducing an intrusion classifier.
replacement: Watchdog monitoring and explicit acknowledgments have long been used to detect forwarding misbehavior [4, 5]. Their observations need careful interpretation. Overhearing confirms a transmission attempt, while reception by the intended next hop remains uncertain. Silence is also ambiguous: the first hop may have failed, the channel may be busy, or the observer may have missed a frame. Penalizing every silence can redirect traffic even when no node is malicious. We study how routing should handle this missing evidence; we do not train an intrusion classifier.

paragraphs.match: Recent work links trust to edge assisted routing [6], optimizer based next hop selection [7], learned trust estimation [8], failure aware deep Q learning [9] and opportunistic forwarder selection [10]. Trust gated reinforcement learning [11] and secure deep reinforcement learning [12] further demonstrate current interest in the interaction between security and routing. Table 1 maps their stated mechanisms to this study. Their reported performance values are not used as directly comparable baselines because the channels, workloads and attack models differ.
replacement: Recent studies combine trust with edge-assisted routing [6], optimizer-based next-hop selection [7], learned trust estimates [8], failure-aware deep Q-learning [9] and opportunistic forwarding [10]. Trust-gated reinforcement learning [11] and secure deep reinforcement learning [12] address related interactions between routing and security. Table 1 compares their stated mechanisms with the question examined here. Differences in channels, workloads and attack models prevent a defensible numerical ranking against those published results.

A subsequent 600-run radio telemetry study also found no corrected architecture advantage and exposed a cost of the active proof mechanism. These negative stages motivated one feedback redesign; they remain available with their raw outputs. The new experiment asks a narrower question: can a receipt assisted passive mechanism replace active proofs without materially degrading a frozen prior control on a new fixture set?

paragraphs.match: The contribution is an auditable feedback-mechanism comparison: first-hop acknowledgment gates evidence, a record retains the strongest observation rather than every duplicate, and missing observations remain censored. A 64-byte application frame contains 12 identifier bytes and 52 payload bytes; lower-layer overhead is additional.
